input.sql: SELECT faa_hub_class_cy, count(*) AS n_airports FROM dim_airport_faa WHERE faa_hub_class = 'L' GROUP BY faa_hub_class_cy

WITH m AS (SELECT f.airport_id, count(DISTINCT t.period_month) AS n_months FROM v_t100_segment t JOIN dim_airport_faa f ON f.airport_id = t.origin_airport_id WHERE f.faa_hub_class = 'L' AND t.year = 2025 AND t.service_type IN ('passenger', 'combi', 'seaplane') AND t.seats > 0 GROUP BY f.airport_id) SELECT min(n_months) AS min_months, max(n_months) AS max_months, count(*) AS n_with_seats FROM m

answer.headline: JFK leads large-hub airports on international seat share in CY2025

claims.text: In {F16.period}, calculated international seat share ({F16.class}) among FAA large hubs ranks from JFK {F16}, MIA {F21}, IAD {F14}, EWR {F11}, LAX {F18}, SFO {F28}, IAH {F15}, BOS {F4}, FLL {F12}, ORD {F23}, HNL {F13}, DFW {F9}, MCO {F20}, SEA {F27}, ATL {F1}, PHL {F24}, DTW {F10}, MSP {F22}, CLT {F6}, TPA {F30}, LAS {F17}, DEN {F8}, PHX {F25}, SLC {F29}, LGA {F19}, AUS {F2}, BWI {F5}, SAN {F26}, BNA {F3}, to DCA {F7}.
The difference in international seat share is {F64} between JFK and MIA and {F63} between JFK and DCA. Both differences are calculated from the shares above.
No two of these international seat shares are identical, so the rank has no ties. The minmax rank score inside this set is {F31} at JFK and {F60} at DCA.

Exploratory reads, not catalog metrics, put the FAA hub-class year at {F61} and the class-L airport count at {F62}. Class-L airports with passenger seats in CY2025 number {F67}, and months with those seats run from {F65} to {F66}.

Because the exploratory month counts run from {F65} to {F66}, the CY2025 shares are not compared across airports that lack months of passenger seats. That does not show that each month contributes equally to the annual share.

Airports toward the top of this list may hold that position because of airline network role and international air-service rights. The ranking does not establish unmet demand, a terminal-capacity constraint, or an investment return.

assumptions: The phrase large hub did not resolve to a city, airport, or region. It is bound to the catalog group filter hub class L, the FAA large-hub code.
Higher international seat share ranks higher. The accompanying score is a minmax rescaling inside this airport set. It is not the seat share itself.
The share uses the catalog formula for {F16.period}: seats on international departing T-100 segments divided by all departing seats.
limitations: Unmet demand, terminal capacity, fares, and profitability are not measured. A higher international seat share is not evidence of any of those.
Only departing segments enter the metric. Arriving international seats are outside it.

This is not an investment screen, so screen scenario flags were not produced. There are no ties in the seat share. Rank scores are relative to this set and would change if airports were added or removed.
Hub-class year, class count, and month counts are exploratory SQL, not catalog metrics. Causes of a high or low share are not identified.
